title: Should You Preach the Gospel in Every Sermon
subtitle: A pastoral case for preaching the gospel in every sermon without it hardening into a formula, with practical ways to move from any biblical text to the cross and the resurrection.

sections.title: The Question Under the Question
sections.body:
The answer is yes. The hard part is everything after the yes.

Most preachers who ask whether the gospel belongs in every sermon are not actually asking a theological question. They are asking a craft question they have disguised as a theological one. They have tried to tack the cross onto the end of a sermon on parenting and felt it land with a thud. They have heard a colleague preach the same three sentences about the death of Christ every Sunday until the words stopped meaning anything. They are not against the gospel. They are against the version of gospel-preaching that has gone numb in their own mouth.

So let us be honest about what is really at stake. The fear is not that you will preach Christ. The fear is that you will preach Him by rote, that the most astonishing news a human being can hear will become the thing your people stop listening to because they can predict it word for word. That fear is worth taking seriously. The cure is not to preach the gospel less. The cure is to preach it like you still believe it.

sections.title: Why It Has to Be Every Week
sections.body:
There are people in your room who will be dead before next Sunday. You do not know which ones.

That alone settles the matter. But there is more. The people who come back every week do not arrive remembering. They arrive having forgotten. They have spent six days being told by every screen and every fear that they are what they produce, that they are loved on the condition of their performance, that they must justify their existence. The world preaches a gospel of merit at them all week, and it is relentless, and it is good at it. Then they walk into your building carrying the weight of it, and you have one hour.

If in that hour you give them only instruction, only ten ways to be a better spouse, only a brave moral challenge, you have sent them back into the week with a heavier pack than they came in with. The law without the gospel does not produce holiness. It produces despair in the honest and pride in the blind. Paul did not assume the Corinthians had moved on from the cross. He resolved to know nothing among them but Christ crucified, and they were not new believers. They were a church. The mature need the gospel as much as the lost. The difference is only that the mature have learned to feel their need for it.

sections.title: Not a Formula. A Reality.
sections.body:
Here is where it goes wrong. The gospel becomes a move instead of a message.

A preacher learns the technique. Spend twenty-five minutes on the text, then in the last four minutes execute the turn to the cross, say the words about the blood and the empty tomb, and sit down. After a year his people can feel the gearshift coming. The sermon was about Jonah and now, on cue, here comes Jesus, stapled to the end like a coupon. The transition is so predictable it has become invisible. They stop hearing it not because they have rejected it but because you have trained them to expect it.

The problem is not repetition. The sun comes up every morning and no one is bored of being alive. The problem is repetition without freshness, the gospel announced the same way, from the same angle, in the same flattened voice, until familiarity has done its quiet work. You can say true things in a tone that makes them sound like fine print. The gospel does not need to be reinvented. It needs to be re-felt, by you first, so that when you announce it on Sunday it carries the heat of a man who got rescued again on Thursday.

sections.title: Let the Text Carry You to Christ
sections.body:
The way out of the formula is to stop bolting the gospel on and start finding it already there.

Every text in the Bible stands in relation to the cross, but not every text gets there the same way. Sometimes the passage shows you a need that only Christ fills. The Law exposes a debt, and you preach the One who paid it. Sometimes the passage shows you a pattern that Christ completes. The temple, the lamb, the king, the exodus, all of it leaning forward toward Him. Sometimes the passage shows you a command you cannot keep, and the good news is not first that you must love your enemy but that He loved His. Bryan Chapell taught a generation to ask where the text reveals our fallen condition and how Christ answers it. That single question kills the formula, because every text answers it differently.

So the road from Genesis runs one way and the road from the Psalms another and the road from Romans another still. When the path changes every week, your people cannot predict the turn, because the turn is honest. You are not performing a transition. You are following a trail the Spirit laid down in the text itself. Christ is not the conclusion you bolt on. He is the destination the passage was already traveling toward.

sections.title: Preach It Like It Saved You
sections.body:
In the end the freshness will not come from a technique. It will come from your knees.

The preacher whose gospel has gone stale almost always has a heart that has gone stale, and no amount of varied phrasing will hide it for long. People can tell the difference between a man reciting good news and a man who cannot get over it. The first thing you owe your congregation on Sunday is not a clever bridge to the cross. It is a preacher who was at the cross on Saturday, undone again by a grace he did not earn and cannot exhaust.

So yes, preach the gospel every week. Preach it from every text, by the road that text provides. Vary the angle, never the substance. But before any of that, go back yourself. Let the death of Christ stop you again. Let the empty tomb make your hands shake. Then walk into the room and tell them what you have just seen.

A formula is what is left when wonder leaves. Do not lose the wonder.
